title: Chicago's great players and the Jabbo Smith versus Armstrong rivalry
summary: Saunders recalls Jabbo Smith sitting in against Louis Armstrong at the Savoy Ballroom; DeMichael tells of Ira Sullivan hearing Jabbo's record.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Well, they had some jazz musicians here, too.

Oh, there's great ones here. You had them down there, but, see, they were like second city or third city or whatever you wanted to call it. But they respected Chicago because they would sit there and listen and every -- ape and everything, because you had Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines and you had all kinds of great musicians. Omer Simeon, like we were saying, and Darnell Howard and Jabbo Smith and all the --
(Inaudible) Jabbo?
Yeah, yeah, right.
Hell of a trumpet player.
Yeah, he's still up in Milwaukee.
Yeah. Yeah, I heard him a couple of years ago, here in town with a college band that was sort of recreating Fletcher Henderson arrangements.
Yeah, right, right.
And his chops were down, but his --
But you still know he could play.
Beautiful ideas.
Yeah, right, right.
Gee, he used to be fa
Oh, he was fabulous.
Was he sort of promoted as the rival to Louis Armstrong?

Yeah, well, I was going to tell you. This happened when Louis was in the Savoy Ballroom, and like, on a Sunday afternoon, this side the bandstand was Clarence Black's band, and over here was Carroll Dickerson. Louis Armstrong was playing in Carroll Dickerson's band, Tubbie Hall and all of them were over here in Clarence Black's band. And this guy came in -- I don't know where, didn't even know him. Boy, and he started blowing that horn, boy, and sweat come over Pop's -- and he was -- and that was one of the greatest nights I think I've ever heard of a rivalry. I

mean, it was a real rivalry, yeah. Right, because he sat in Clarence Black's band, Jabbo did, and then Louis, who naturally, you know -- and boy, that was really something. And he was playing then, Jabbo was.
Oh, yeah, Jabbo --
And this is really what -- that was my first introduction to him, you know.
Ira Sullivan used to be a neighbor of mine (inaudible).
(Recording interrupted.)
And Ira came over to my house one day.
Yeah.
And I said, did you ever hear of Jabbo Smith? He says no, so I put on this old Jabbo Smith record, the Boston Scuffle.
Yeah.
And Ira just fell on the floor.
No kidding.
He didn't know anybody played like that. He was playing bebop.

Right, right, right, and he -- on that particular night, you know, I mean, it was just such an intense rival and he was intent on showing his ability, and this guy after playing all of that, he picked up the trombone, man, and started playing, and played the hell out of it.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Too bad there weren't tape recorders back then.
Oh, yeah, right, right, right.
In Kansas City with those sessions.
Yeah.
